Chess club note, Saturday. Nikita Joshi, coach.
Gautam (16) is my hardest worker. He tracks his rating every day on a chart taped inside his notebook. When the district secretary praised him last month, he glowed for a week. He wants first place at the state juniors, and he has told me more than once that second "doesn't count."
This week he lost a game he should have drawn. He didn't cry. He went very still, packed up without shaking hands properly, and came in the next morning with red eyes, saying he had played through the night. He has skipped every rest day I've set.
I admire his drive. It has taken him far. But I worry that he only feels he is worth something when the chart goes up.
Next: I will play one game a week with him with no rating and no result recorded, and I will talk to his parents about sleep before the tournament.

qa.a: On a chart taped inside his notebook.

qa.q: What does Gautam's saying that second 'doesn't count' reveal about how he sees himself?
qa.a: It reveals that he measures his worth by results, so anything less than first feels like failure rather than progress.

qa.q: Which of Nikita Joshi's next steps might help Gautam most, and why?
qa.a: The unrated weekly game might help most, because it lets him enjoy chess without his worth riding on the result, giving room for rest and loss.

qa.a: The opponent might have felt uneasy or slighted, not knowing how heavily the loss weighed on Gautam.

grounding: It shows a teenager who pushes for top results and praise, feeling worthy only when he wins, which drives effort but leaves no room for rest or failure.

Friday night
Second prize. SECOND. At the district science fair, my water-filter model came second to a solar cooker. The principal shook the winner's hand and said, "This is the future." To me she said, "Good effort."
Good effort. I worked till two every night for three weeks. I skipped Parul's birthday. I didn't even go down for dinner half the time.
On the bus back I stared out of the window so nobody would see my face. Parul sat next to me and said, "Vasudha, it's a great model. You're more than a trophy." I nodded but I didn't believe her. If I'm not first, what am I?
Mumma made my favourite kadhi tonight and called me her clever girl. I couldn't eat it.
I know I'm tired. My head aches. But the inter-state fair is in four months, and I've already started planning version two.
Vasudha

qa.a: A solar cooker.

qa.a: She measures her worth by being first, so coming second made her feel like nothing, whatever her friend said.

qa.q: What choice could Vasudha make before starting version two, and why might it help?
qa.a: She could rest and eat properly for a while, and let herself enjoy the model she made, so her effort doesn't cost her sleep, friends and health.

qa.q: How might Parul feel after Vasudha skipped her birthday and then didn't believe her comfort?
qa.a: Parul might feel hurt and helpless, caring about Vasudha but unable to reach past her need to win.

grounding: It shows a teenager who feels her worth through first place and praise from respected people, pushing hard but leaving no room for rest or failure.

Afreen Apa,
You'll have seen my photos. Your little brother is head of the cultural committee now. I stood because the fest was always run by the same three seniors and nobody else got a say. I wanted juniors and day scholars to have a voice.

Apa, how do you want respect without wanting to control everyone? Tell me when you call on Sunday.

I'm Gautam, Jaya Didi's younger brother. She's twenty-one and studies physics in Delhi, and this year she came home to Patna for Chhath even though her exams were close.
She didn't just come for the food. She scrubbed the brass pots with Ma, shaped thekua with her own hands, and kept the fast with the women of the house, no water from the evening before. At the ghat, she stood in the river at sunset holding the soop with fruit and a lamp, eyes closed, lips moving.
Her college friends had teased her on video call. "A physics student standing in a river?" She laughed and said, "I know how the sun works. This isn't about that."
I asked her later why she bothered. She said, "When I'm here, I know exactly who I am."
I don't know everything she felt out there in the cold water. But she looked more peaceful than I've seen her all year.

qa.a: The soop with fruit and a lamp.

qa.q: What does Jaya's reply, 'When I'm here, I know exactly who I am,' suggest about what the ritual means to her?
qa.a: It suggests the festival gives her belonging and a sense of identity that her busy life in Delhi does not, whatever her friends think.

Day one. The evening before the Ashadhi wari, Omkar, twenty, packed a cloth bag in his family's Pune flat: a white kurta, a small cymbal, his grandfather's old copy of abhangs. His college friend Tushar watched, puzzled. "You're walking with the pilgrims? You, the robotics guy?"
"Every year since I was eight," Omkar said. "With Baba. Two days."
Day two. On the road out of the city, thousands walked together, singing. Omkar's feet hurt. An old man he had never met shared his bhakri with him. When Baba started a verse his own father used to sing, Omkar's voice cracked. He felt, for a moment, part of something enormous and very old.
Day three. Back at the hostel, Tushar asked, "Don't you think all that's a bit outdated?"
Omkar thought for a while. "Some of it, maybe. I argue with Baba about some things. But when I walk, I'm connected to everyone who walked before me. I'm not giving that up."

I'm Jahnavi, Rafiq's younger sister. My brother is twenty-five, and he's the most careful person I know.
Last year his college friend offered him a place in a travel start-up. More excitement, maybe more money one day. Rafiq said no and took the clerk's post in the railway office. Steady salary, fixed hours, a pension.
On salary day, he sits at the table with a notebook and divides the money into envelopes: rent, Ammi's medicines, my college fees, and one marked 'emergencies.' He never touches that one.
When I asked if he regretted the start-up, he said, "When Abbu's shop shut down, we didn't know about rent for a year. I never want you or Ammi to feel that again."
Most days he seems calm, even content. But some nights I hear him awake, checking the envelopes again. I don't know if that's worry or just habit.

qa.a: Emergencies.

qa.a: It suggests the fear from that uncertain year still drives him, and he values safety for his family more than chances for himself.

qa.a: It gives them steady support for rent, medicines and fees; it may cost him some excitement and bring him restless nights of worry.

qa.a: She sees his care and calm and feels protected, but she also notices his late-night checking and wonders whether it is worry.

March. Sabina, twenty-five, had two offers: cabin crew with a new airline, or a junior officer's post at the district cooperative bank. The airline meant travel and adventure. The bank meant fixed hours near home. She thought of her father's hands, shaking the year his job ended, and signed with the bank.
July. The monsoon flooded her brother Bhupen's small shop. He was frantic. Sabina could help him buy new stock from her steady salary and savings, and Ammi slept through the night for the first time in weeks. Sabina felt a deep, quiet calm. This was why.
November. A school friend posted photos from the airline: Singapore, Dubai, a smile in uniform. Sabina scrolled for a long time. That evening she felt a small ache and a worry: had she chosen fear over life? Then Bhupen called to say the shop had its best week yet. She smiled, still a little unsure, and put the phone down.

In a café in Toronto, Javier, twenty-six, turned his cup round and round. The offer from Berlin had come: a design job he'd dreamed of, a new life. But his parents in Guadalajara were getting older, and his father had asked, not for the first time, if he'd come home and help with the family bakery.
His friend Chen listened. "So what matters most?"
"That's the thing," Javier said. "Freedom says Berlin. Security says the bakery. Tradition says family comes first. They can't all win." He took a breath. "For this decision, right now, being near my parents matters most. I'll go home. Maybe Berlin comes again, maybe not."
Chen smiled. "You know I made the opposite call. I left Shanghai."
"I know. And you were right, for you." Javier meant it. "Your parents are well. Your brother is there. Mine isn't the same situation."
He paid for both coffees and walked out into the cold, sad and clear at once.

qa.a: From Berlin.

qa.a: He felt sad about letting go of the Berlin dream but clear and settled about his choice to go home.

I'm Devika. I sit next to Wasim in Class 4, and he's funny, but he runs everything like a shop.
In art on Tuesday, I forgot my sharpener. I asked to borrow his. He said, "Okay, but I'll use your blue crayon for the whole class." I said fine.
Then the new boy, Ronit, asked Wasim for his eraser because he'd rubbed a hole in his page. Wasim looked at Ronit's pencil box, which was almost empty. "What will you give me?" Ronit had nothing. So Wasim said, "Then no." He didn't say it meanly. He said it like a rule.
After class I asked him why. He shrugged. "If I give free, then everyone takes free. I'll share my pencil if you share your eraser. That's fair."
I don't know if he even noticed Ronit's face. Ronit had to fix his page with his finger.

I have a proposal, and I need your help with Papa. You know I've been asking for a phone for a year. Payal and everyone in my class have one.
So here is my offer. If you convince Papa, I will:
1. Massage your feet every night before bed.
2. Wash the dinner dishes on weekdays.
3. Read the newspaper to you on Sundays, even the boring pages.
4. Get above 80 in maths.
That is a very good deal, Dadi. You will have happy feet and a clean kitchen. I will have a phone. Everyone wins.
I know Papa listens to you more than anyone.
Please think about it and reply by Friday.
Your favourite granddaughter (don't tell Chhavi),
Indu

qa.q: What will Indu read to Dadi on Sundays?
qa.a: The newspaper, even the boring pages.

qa.q: What does Indu's list of promises suggest she thinks about helping at home?
qa.a: It suggests she sees chores and caring for Dadi as payment for the phone, a practical trade rather than something she does out of care yet.

qa.q: If you were Dadi, what might you say back to Indu?
qa.a: Dadi could thank her for the honest offer and suggest that the foot massages and newspaper would be lovely even without a phone, nudging her from deal toward care.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel when she reads this letter?
qa.a: Dadi might feel amused and touched by the effort and honesty, while noticing that the kindness is being offered as a price.

grounding: It shows a teenager who offers chores and caring tasks as a price for a phone, a practical and honest deal that is not yet care for the family.

subtopic: Kohlberg self-interest stage
passage:
In the marketing office in Amman, Yara, twenty-six, stayed late to help Nkechi finish her slides for the director. Not because Nkechi was drowning, though she was. Because Nkechi ate lunch with the director twice a week.
On the bus home, Yara opened a note on her phone. Nkechi: owes me one, big. Under it were other entries: Omar covered my Friday, I owe him a coffee. Hana helped with Excel, returned. It was all very fair. She never took more than she gave.
A month later, Nkechi stopped at Yara's desk, eyes red. "My father's in hospital back home. I just needed to tell someone."
Yara said, "Oh no, I'm sorry," and then didn't know what else to say. She realised she knew nothing about Nkechi's father, or anyone's family, or what anyone here loved. Nkechi nodded and walked away.
That night Yara looked at her list for a long time.

qa.q: How often did Nkechi eat lunch with the director?
qa.a: Twice a week.

qa.q: What did Yara realise when Nkechi told her about her father?
qa.a: She realised she knew nothing about Nkechi's life or anyone else's, because she had only ever kept track of favours.

qa.q: What might Yara choose to do differently after looking at her list?
qa.a: She could start getting to know colleagues as people, asking about their lives and helping sometimes without writing it down.

qa.q: How might Nkechi have felt when Yara had nothing more to say?
qa.a: Nkechi probably felt lonely and let down, having reached out in pain to someone who could only offer a polite sentence.

grounding: It shows an adult who helps a colleague for future gain and keeps a ledger of favours, dealing fairly but finding her work relationships thin.

subtopic: Kohlberg self-interest stage
passage:
At the IT company in Pune, Mridul, twenty-five, had a rule: help people who can help you back. So when Sumit, from the team that decided next quarter's project allocation, asked for help fixing a stubborn bug, Mridul stayed two hours. Later he added a line in the notebook in his drawer: Sumit, 2 hours, allocation.
He was scrupulously fair. Whenever someone helped him, he paid it back within a week, exactly. People called him reliable.
In October, at the team's lunch table, everyone was passing Sumit's phone around: photos of his newborn daughter. People asked her name, told stories about their own kids, laughed. Mridul realised he hadn't known Sumit's wife was pregnant. He hadn't known Priti from testing had a son, or that Kiran had just moved house.
He smiled and said, "Congratulations," and ate his biryani in silence. Back at his desk, he opened the notebook and couldn't find a single entry that told him who anyone was.

qa.q: What did Mridul write in the notebook after helping Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit, 2 hours, allocation.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling as he ate his biryani in silence?
qa.a: He felt left out and uneasy, realising that everyone else knew each other's lives while he knew only who owed whom.

qa.q: What choice could Mridul make after that lunch?
qa.a: He could start asking colleagues about their lives and helping without tracking the payoff, so his fairness comes with real connection.

qa.q: How do Mridul's colleagues seem to see him?
qa.a: They see him as reliable and fair, but perhaps not as someone to share personal news with, since his help always seems to be a trade.

grounding: It shows an adult who helps colleagues only when it may pay off and keeps a ledger of favours, dealing fairly but ending up with thin relationships.
